title: Word Tree With Prefix Search
statement:
Build a store of lowercase words that answers two questions quickly: was this exact word added, and does any added word start with this text?

  • Trie() creates an empty store.
  • insert(word) adds word. Adding the same word again changes nothing.
  • search(word) returns true only if word itself was added. Being the start of a longer added word is not enough.
  • startsWith(prefix) returns true if at least one added word begins with prefix. A word counts as a prefix of itself.

Each call should cost time proportional to the length of its argument, not to the number of stored words.

Tests are written as a list of operations and their arguments; the first operation creates the store. The expected output has one entry per operation (null where nothing is returned).

examples.out: [null, null, false, true, true, null, true]
examples.why: "pain" lies on the path of "paint", but it is not a word until it is inserted on its own. The tree must mark where words end, not just store paths.
A whole word is its own prefix. "mat" shares "ma" with "map" but then branches off, and "ma" is only a path.

constraints: Words and prefixes use lowercase English letters only
hints: A set answers search in O(L). The hard part is startsWith: how do you avoid checking every stored word?
Words that start the same way can share storage for that start. Picture a tree where each edge is one letter and each path from the root spells a prefix.

Each node maps a letter to a child node and has a flag saying "a word ends here". insert walks and creates nodes; search walks and checks the flag; startsWith walks and only checks that the path exists.

explain.intuition:
Store the words as a tree of letters. The root is the empty string; each child edge adds one letter, so every node stands for one prefix. "map" and "mat" share the nodes for "m" and "ma" and split only at the last letter. Now startsWith("ma") is a walk of two steps from the root, no matter how many words are stored. This is how autocomplete in a search box can suggest completions while you type.

A path existing only proves that some word passes through that prefix. To know a word ends there, each node carries an end flag, set by insert on the last node. That one flag is the whole difference between search and startsWith.
steps: A node has kids, a map from letter to child node, and a boolean end.
insert(word): start at the root. For each letter, go to the child for that letter, creating it if missing. Set end = true on the last node.
Write one helper walk(s) that follows the letters of s from the root and returns the node reached, or nothing if a letter has no child.
pitfalls: Returning "the path exists" from search. After inserting "paint", search("pain") must still be false.
Setting end on every node along the path during insert instead of only the last one. Then every prefix of an inserted word looks like a word.
Storing every prefix of every word in a set. It works, but a word of length L adds L strings of total length about L²/2, which explodes for long words.

complexity.time: O(L) per call, where L is the argument's length

solutions.title: Set of words, scan for prefixes
solutions.idea: search is a set lookup. startsWith checks every stored word, so it costs O(number of words · L).
solutions.time: O(L) insert and search, O(W · L) startsWith

solutions.title: Trie of letter nodes
solutions.idea: Each node maps a letter to a child and marks whether a word ends there. Every call walks at most one path from the root.

followups: Add countPrefix(prefix), the number of stored words that start with it. What would you keep in each node to answer in O(L)?
Add remove(word). How do you delete nodes that no longer lead to any word without breaking other words?
Only letters a–z are allowed. When is a fixed array of 26 children better than a map, and when is it worse?
